intro: Every change to the record, the stage ladder or the site, with absolute dates. Newest first. The Story page on the site renders this file.

items: **An automated check for quoted recordings, proposed for John to ratify (2026-10-17).** John ruled earlier the same day that he will not check quoted passages by ear and that automatic captions are acceptable, and asked for a reliable automated check instead. The rule, in the record layout under "Checking quoted recordings": a quoted passage from a recording counts as checked when YouTube's automatic captions and a local Whisper transcription of the audio agree on the quoted words (case, punctuation and filler sounds ignored); a difference is flagged with both readings and settled by a larger local Whisper model, then an official transcript, then the speaker's own text, and stays open if none settles it. It checks the words, not what a claim means, and never changes a claim's date, status or account. A claim carries the result in a small table (`transcript_check`) and its `checked_how` opens with one of three set sentences, which the export script now checks. `scripts/check_quotes.py` applies the rule (how to run it: `docs/check-quotes.md`); it fetches captions and audio, transcribes the quoted stretch, prints the table and never writes to the record.

**The seven recorded claims, run through it on 2026-10-17** with Whisper large-v3-turbo as the second transcript: all seven quoted phrases are found in both transcripts, the 2018 film's only after a full copy of it was found (the first upload is now a 3-minute clip; its captions are still readable, the new link has the audio, and the quoted line is at 1:11:49 to 1:11:50 in both; the link on the entry now points to the full copy). One extra passage was checked as well: the audience answer at the Neuralink launch of 2019 (about 01:22:15), where the captions read "sympotic", the turbo model "sympathetic" and a larger model (Whisper large-v3) "symbiotic", which is the entry's reading; the entry is marked settled by the larger model. The "still to check" lines about listening are gone from six entries; the Dubai 2017 entry keeps one for a different reason (its account says "around ten bits per second", where both transcripts have him say "10 bits per second or 100 if you're being generous"; the account is unchanged). No claim's date, status or account changed. The Whisper settings for the check use no random retries, so the same audio reads the same each time (an earlier run with the default retries once read "bandwidth" as "bandless" in the Seo talk). The claims page now describes the check in one sentence.

**The five lifespan-and-repair entries are linked to their matching leaves on Outrunning Ageing** (outrunningageing.com, the sibling site that asks when repair overtakes ageing, live since 2026-10-17), both ways on this side: a drug makes people live longer in good health; partially resetting cells reverses ageing in a living animal; a drug clears aged cells from a person's body; an organ from a gene-edited pig keeps a person alive; a printed or lab-grown organ works in a person for a year. Each entry now carries the id of its leaf there in a new optional field, `sibling` (the same name and the same idea as the field those five leaves have carried pointing here since 2026-10-16), with a dated revision and a note; each entry's page shows one line linking to the leaf's page there; the export carries the id and the address through. Checked on 2026-10-17 against the sibling's public records: all five pairs sit on the same rung with the same date and the same record, so no stage changed and the headline count stays at 28 of 35. The field and a second rule, that an upgrade carrying a field the layout does not list is refused, are proposed in the record layout document and wait on John. Done in a cloud session, so it arrives as a pull request rather than a commit on main.

**The weekly reading gains the stage-agreement check.** After the upgrades are read, the scanner runs a new script (`scripts/sibling_check.py`) that reads each linked leaf's record from the sibling's public repository and prints both stages, dates and records with a verdict per pair. A pair that differs, or a leaf that cannot be read, makes that upgrade's item a flagged one for John; the scanner never copies the other site's stage, because a rung here moves only on the kind of record the entry names. The procedure, the standalone instruction for the scheduled run and the decisions list (item 12, proposed) say so.

**John ruled the three calls the claims-and-bandwidth work left open ("yes to all", 2026-10-17; each question was raised 2026-10-16).** The claims page keeps its name, "The claims". The 2006 BrainGate paper stays on the bandwidth series as its starting mark with no rate, because it states none: it shows in the table and not on the chart. Neuralink's own 8.0 bits a second (2024-05-08) belongs on the pointing chart, shown as a hollow dot and labelled in the legend and the table as the maker's own release, with the best peer-reviewed figure (4.16, Stanford, 2017) named beside it. The page and the chart already did all three, so nothing on the site changed; the rulings are recorded in the decisions table of the record layout document.

**The listening pass.** Every claim held on a recording was checked again on 2026-10-17. All seven recordings turned out to have automatic captions only, including the 2017 Dubai one, which the record had called human-made-looking. Six were transcribed again from the audio by a second, separate speech-recognition program (OpenAI's Whisper): Musk in Dubai 2017, Harari at Davos 2018, Musk at the Neuralink launch 2019, the Neuralink update 2020, DJ Seo's talk 2022, and Musk in Dubai 2025 (the whole talk). In every case the two machines agree on the quoted phrase and on the account, so no quoted words and no claim changed; four timestamp ranges were widened by a few seconds (Dubai 2017, the launch, the 2020 update, Seo) because the two machines place the phrase up to three seconds apart. No person has listened to any of them, and the site now says so: each of the six carries a "still to check" line, and each names the exact stretch to listen to. One word is left to an ear: in the launch-event audience answer the captions read "sympotic" and the second program "sympathetic", and the entry reads "symbiosis".

**One correction from the listening pass.** The Harari entry said the word "hackable" is absent from his Davos talk of 2020. It is not: he says "We are now hackable animals" at about 12:13, and the automatic captions had it as "packable animals". That is very probably where the circulating phrase "humans are now hackable animals" comes from. The 2018 entry stands (the word occurs nowhere in the 2018 talk, which a second transcription of the whole recording confirms); only its note about the 2020 talk is corrected. The 2020 talk is not entered as a claim; that is John's call.

**Two claims could not be listened to.** The 2018 film "Do You Trust This Computer?": the upload the record linked is now a 3-minute clip of other material, not the film, so the recording cannot be reached; the quoted line matches CNBC's own transcription of 2018-04-06 word for word, and the entry says it rests on captions and that transcription. The Schneider Financial Times piece stays headline-only behind the paywall. One post was upgraded: Musk's "If you can't beat em, join em" was read on 2026-10-17 from X's own embed data for the post, which confirms the words and puts the posting at 07:01 universal time on 2020-07-09 (00:01 Pacific).

**The two open checks from 2026-10-16.** The first mitochondrial-donation child's birth date: still no source from the clinic or the authors. The paper and the authors' later commentary give only his age (7 and 11 months); the clinic's pages carry press clippings; the day 2016-04-06 rests on CNN, The Guardian and New York magazine of 2016-09-27 and 28. The entry's note now says exactly that, and the stage and the date stand. Vidal's 1977 maze paper: still only the abstract can be read; no open copy exists; the entry's note records the second attempt and the date stands. The third item from the first reading, the 2016 Pittsburgh touch paper, was settled on 2026-10-16 and was not re-read in full here; its first-publication date of 2016-10-13 was confirmed from Europe PMC.

**The top bar carries short handles** (Branches · Reading · Claims · Story | Method · Disagree · Source; Home drops, the site's name is the home link), the full plain names staying as the page titles and in the footer, under rule 4.7 of the tracker pattern John ruled on 2026-10-16 after seeing the three live bars side by side. The seven links now sit on one row beside the site's name at 1280 pixels, so the collapse band up to 1320 pixels added earlier the same evening for the long names is gone and the standard's own collapse at 820 pixels is enough.

The claims are on the site. "The claims" (/claims/) sits in the heavier tier of the top bar, as the tracker pattern John ruled on 2026-10-16 puts the page a site is built around. It shows the twenty-seven claims from the project's claims log in date order, 2000 to 2026, each with its one exact phrase, the plain account with the hedges kept, the source link and how the words were checked, and its marking in words where it is held on coverage only or where a version that circulates has no primary source; beside them, on the same page, what the seven branches have actually reached and the headline count, so the gap between talk and delivery is visible (the pattern's rule 6.4). The entries moved from the TimeAssembler document into the repository as one file per claim under data/claims/, nothing added or dropped, with John's three sourcing rulings of 2026-10-16 kept as the document recorded them: the two Nicolelis entries and the Wait But Why entry held as unsourced, coverage only, with no quoted words; the Schneider 2019 piece kept as a claim with its fiction framing as a hedge; the Warwick 2003 paper dated by the paper with the implant's date beside it. The one speaker looked for and not found, and the fourteen leads noted and not yet checked, are kept with the record and shown at the foot of the page.

The brain-to-machine bandwidth series exists: data/bandwidth.toml, eight dated figures from 2006 to 2024, each in the unit its source used, with who measured it, in whom, whether it was repeated, and whether it came from a peer-reviewed paper or the maker's own release; every figure read in its primary source on 2026-10-16 (the two claims not fully readable are in the points' verify lists). Two measures are kept apart, text out of the head (words a minute, with characters shown as words at five a word) and pointing at a screen (bits a second), each plotted on the link-to-machines page as dots with a stepped line for the best so far and dashed lines for the rates a reader already has: speech in conversation at 160 words a minute, a fast typist at 120, typing on a phone at 115 characters a minute, an engineer with a mouse at about 10 bits a second, speech as information at 39. The best figure so far for text is 78 words a minute (San Francisco, August 2023), about half the speed of talking with one word in four wrong; for pointing, 8.0 bits a second (Neuralink's own figure, May 2024) against a peer-reviewed best of 4.16 (Stanford, 2017). The 2006 BrainGate paper is on the series as its starting mark with no rate, because it states none.

The record layout gains the claim record (one file per claim, named by date then slug, with a sourced or unsourced status and the paraphrase table the charter asks for) and the bandwidth series (measures, points and baselines), both validated by the export script before anything is written. The method page's "what is not here yet" now names only the weekly reading.

The hearing gene therapy moved from first human to in clinical use on the FDA's accelerated approval of Otarmeni (2026-04-23), which the first weekly reading found the entry had missed; ruled by John on 2026-10-16, with a dated revision, the first-human record kept in earlier stages, and Otarmeni, OTOF and lunsotogene parvec added as watch terms. The headline count is unchanged at 28 of 35; the five-rung totals are now 4, 3, 18, 7, 3.

The weekly reading built: a procedure in plain words (docs/weekly-reading.md, adapted from The Belt Equation's scan plan and procedure, every design choice with its confidence and an alternative, the schedule proposed), the reading record's layout in the record layout document (one file per run under data/readings/, never edited, four verdicts: quiet, noted, stage change, flagged) with the export script refusing any record that breaks it, and an optional list of extra search terms (`watch`) on each upgrade. The scanner may move a stage one rung on a record of the kind the upgrade names, and may not touch a test, a settler, a verify list or the headline rung; everything else is a flagged item for John.

The first reading, done by hand on 2026-10-16 (record at data/readings/2026-10-16.toml): all 35 upgrades read, 75 searches, none moved, two noted (the first United States patient with a bone-anchored arm with implanted nerve and muscle electrodes, 2026-09-17, in a study and not under an approval; and the Australian regulator's page the psychedelic entry could not load earlier in the day, read tonight and matching the entry, a claim the verify session cleared the same evening), one flagged for John: the FDA approved Regeneron's Otarmeni, the first gene therapy for a genetic hearing loss, on 2026-04-23, so the hearing gene therapy entry's note that no regulator had approved one is wrong and the entry would move to in clinical use. Two claims still to check were looked at and not settled (the first mitochondrial-donation child's exact birth date; whether the 2016 Pittsburgh touch paper itself includes the robotic hand), and a third was found supported but unread (Vidal's 1977 maze-by-brain-signal paper as an earlier first human for the scalp headset).

The site: the home page's last-checked strip now reads the latest reading (the date written out, how many upgrades were read, what moved, what waits on John); a "This week's reading" page at /reading/ in the top bar's heavier tier, with every run newest first, the items grouped by branch, the flagged items waiting on John, and a key to the four verdicts; each upgrade page shows its last three readings. The page, the strip and the verdict badges are copied from The Belt Equation's Radar with a comment saying so. The top bar, now six page names, sits tighter below 1320 pixels and collapses behind the menu button below 1080, as The Quiet Galaxy's does.

The scheduled run: docs/weekly-reading-prompt.md is the standalone instruction a fresh session follows, and a scheduled task on John's Mac ("Upgrade Tree: weekly reading of the upgrades against the news", Sundays at 18:00 Pacific) opens the repository and follows it. The task can be switched off in the app's Scheduled section; moving it to a cloud routine so it does not need the Mac awake is proposed, not done.

Home page checked against the tracker pattern's type roles after the family design review of 2026-10-16 (the sans for an answer, the monospace with aligned figures for a number, the serif only for prose): the count "28 of 35" is in the monospace with aligned figures and its claim in the sans, so nothing changed; the question under them stays in the serif, as the parent site's does. The picture at 1280 pixels is `docs/home-page-2026-10-16-type-check.png`, taken after the Plate skin landed, in the dark theme.

The site wears its own skin, "Plate": warm paper, ink and one plate green, with the human figure standing on the page between double rules like a plate in an anatomy book, light by default (dark kept for readers who ask for it), no starfield, no galaxy, no web font. Proposed with mock-ups in the Sentient Horizons design standard (`design/proposals/upgrade-tree-skin-2026-10-16.md`) and ruled by John on 2026-10-16 after the standard split into a shared skeleton and a skin per site. The stylesheet is now `skin.css` (this site's tokens) plus the shared `shell.css` 2.0.1 plus the site's own rules; the starfield component is gone; the favicon and the browser's theme colour take the paper and the green. The skeleton copy also fixes a bug the whole family had: in the light theme a solid button's text took the link colour and all but vanished. Pictures before and after in `docs/site-2026-10-16-*.jpg`.

The six claims written from memory were checked against their primary records on 2026-10-16. Three are settled and their notes removed: the Australian regulator's notice of 3 February 2023 on psilocybin and MDMA (in force 1 July 2023) says what the entry says; the company's own newsroom links its embryo-product launch release, dated 4 June 2025; and the 2016 Pittsburgh paper does include touch from a prosthetic hand's sensors (84.3 per cent of finger touches identified), so the touch entry's record stands. One moved: the headset entry's in-wide-use date goes from 2015-12-31 to 2014-08-28, the earliest dated copy in the Internet Archive of the maker's page that says over a million of its chips are in circulation (revision recorded on the entry). Two remain open, each reworded to say what was tried: the birth date of the first child born with a donor's mitochondria (the paper gives no birth date, so 2016-04-06 still rests on press coverage) and Vidal's 1977 paper (only its abstract is readable, and it does not mention the maze). No stage changed. The count is unchanged at 28 of 35.

Home page first screen redesigned to the tracker pattern's section 1.3 order in The Belt Equation's layout: the count in the largest type with its claim and the five-rung totals, then the question, one paragraph, the last-checked strip and two buttons ("What has been tried?", "Who is counting"), with the figure beside them; the whole first screen fits at 1280 by 720. Asked by John on 2026-10-16 so a new reader meets the answer before the question.

The real list written: thirty-five upgrades across the seven branches, from the first leaf list John ruled on 2026-10-16 (the charter calls it thirty-six, but names thirty-five; the count is the charter's to correct). The four example entries are gone, their three ids kept and rewritten (the sight implant, the ageing drug, the gene-edited child, the wireless brain chip). Every stage above idea only carries a date and a primary record (a paper, a regulator's database entry or notice, or the institution's own release naming the patient), each checked against the record itself on 2026-10-16; the six claims not yet checked against their record are in the entries' verify lists. The headline count is 28 of 35 at a first human or beyond: 4 idea only, 3 shown in animals, 19 first human, 6 in clinical use, 3 in wide use.

Six rungs differ from the charter's expectation, each explained in the entry's notes: the bone-anchored limb with nerve control sits at first human, not in clinical use (only the bone anchor is approved); the fear-memory treatment sits at first human, not shown in animals (a 2009 human study erased a conditioned fear); the artificial womb sits at idea only, not shown in animals (no mammal has gone from conception to birth outside a body, and the test says so); and three first humans are earlier than the charter had in mind (the visual cortex implant, 1968 not 2018; the wired cursor implant, 1998 not 2004; the memory implant, 2012 not 2018). The wireless brain chip's first human moved from Neuralink's 2024 implant to a fully implanted Dutch system reported in 2016.

The record layout gains a fourth horizon value, "top", for entries already in wide use, so the page does not say "longer than 20 years, if ever" about a finished thing; and a dating rule: an event the record itself dates (a birth, an operation) takes the event's date, a study takes its publication date.
The home page already showed the totals for all five rungs directly under the headline count, as John ruled on 2026-10-16; checked, not changed.

The brain-to-machine bandwidth series is still to come: the record layout has no place for it yet (it is to be its own data file, not a field on an upgrade), so the speech and cursor entries carry their figures in their notes as the series' first two points, in the units their papers use.

The top bar and footer renamed to the page names of the tracker pattern John ruled on 2026-10-16: the spine is Home, Branches and "The story so far"; the lighter tier is "How the numbers are worked out" (the method page, retitled to match, still mostly about how a stage is decided) and "Disagree with something". "This week's reading" is the name for the weekly scan page once one exists; there is none yet, so the home page's "Last checked" strip stays plain text and will link there when the page comes.

theupgradetree.com and upgradetree.com, registered by John on Cloudflare the same evening, attached to the site as custom domains, with www.theupgradetree.com, upgradetree.com and www.upgradetree.com forwarding to the same page at theupgradetree.com. A small Worker in front of the static files (`site/worker/redirect.js`, the Quiet Galaxy's way) does the forwarding; the workers.dev preview address keeps serving the site directly.

First version of the website built: a home page with the question, the human figure shaded by the furthest stage reached under each of the seven branches, and the headline count; a page per branch; a page per upgrade with its stage ladder; the Method, Story and Disagree pages. Deployed to the workers.dev preview address; the domains (theupgradetree.com and upgradetree.com) are John's to buy and attach.

The record layout written (docs/upgrade-schema.md): seven branches in data/branches.toml and one TOML file per branch, each upgrade carrying a stage from the five-rung ladder (idea only, shown in animals, first human, in clinical use, in wide use) with the date and public record that put it there. No probabilities, by John's ruling of 2026-10-16.

Four example upgrades seeded, one each under Senses, Lifespan and repair, Inheritance and The link to machines, marked "EXAMPLE ENTRY" in their notes. They show the record shape; the real list is being written from the project charter in TimeAssembler and replaces them. Every date in them written from memory is listed in the entry's `verify` field.
Repository created on GitHub (jfredson/upgrade-tree, public) with the MIT licence for code and CC BY 4.0 for the record.
